messages.body_plain:
Dear Phil

Thanks a lot for you answer! I really appreciate a lot your fantastic job with mirt and avaliability to answer our questions in this group !

I still have a hard time understanding how item loadings will be valid in this case. Let me make another example trying my question to make more clear what I think:

Suppose I have two booklets:

Bkl A: 1 to 10 (language) 11 to 20 (math)  t
Bkl B  21 to 30 (language) and 31 to 40 (math)

One sample answer Bkl A and another sample answer bklB

So there is no items in common. Suppose the true model is a bi-factor with a general factor and two group factors (language and math).

Having this setup I guess that mirt fa will report  four group factors right ?

How can it identify that items 1-10 and 21-30 are measuring the same group factors since it doesn't have any observation (response vectors) with items 1-10 with 21 and 30 ?

Thanks a lot

Ricardo

On Friday, October 19, 2018 at 10:47:41 AM UTC-3, Phil Chalmers wrote:
> On Thu, Oct 18, 2018 at 10:37 AM 'Ricardo Primi' via mirt-package <mirt-p...@googlegroups.com> wrote:
> > Dear Phil
> >
> > I have a question about results of item factor analysis reported in mirt.
> >
> > Suppose I have 3 booklets of items .
> >
> > Bkl1:  items 1 -20
> > Bkl2: items 11-40 (items 11 to 20 shared with booklet 1)
> > Bkl3: items 31-50 (items 31 to 40 shared with booklet 2)
> >
> > And a random sample of students answering each booklet. Sample A of 1000 students answer bkl1,  Sample B of other 1000 students answer bkl2 and .. so forth
> >
> > Note that I don’t have all pairwise combinations . I can’t compute correlations between items  1-10 with to 21 to 50
> > So I can’t factor analyze in a classical way because I don’t have the full inter-correaltion of items
> >
> > But if I run mirt with two factors, i guess I can have loadings of all items in the two factors right ?
>
> Correct. mirt uses a full information estimator, so the pairwise patterns do not matter. So long as the missing data are missing at random, which they are by design here, then your estimates will be valid.
>
> >  Are these loadings affected by the structure of the booklets? Are these loadings interpretable ?
>
> No, they are not affected. Loadings have the same interpretation as always.
>
> > Are they similar to what I wold see if I had full test to all subjects and had a full intercorrelation matrix ?
>
> Yes, again, FIML estimator.
>
> > I guess you only  analyze covariance between items that you have concomitant data on response vectors right ?
>
> I suppose so, but that sounds like you may be asking a different question. Regardless, FIML estimators make no assumption about the uni/bi/tri/.... variate correlations since all components are computed row-wise for each unique observation in isolation.
>
> Phil
>
> >
> > If you have any reference that explains how this is done it will be very helpful
> >
> > Best
> >
> > Ricardo

On Sat, Nov 3, 2018 at 3:31 AM Conal Monaghan <conal.m...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi Phil,
> Thanks for the detailed reply. Your suggestions are helpful and what i was thinking. Matching difficulty between the tasks is easy using mirt, however, given they have not been equated how comparable are the difficulty parameters between the tasks. I.e. if all three tasks have an average difficulty of 0, what can we infer about their equivilence?

Very little could be said, unfortunately, due to identification constraints. By convention we fix the mean/variance of the latent traits to 0/1, and therefore identify the difficulty of the items based entirely on this constraint (in a relative way). So, difficulties are only interpreted in isolation relative to these traits, and can't be compared across groups without some type of equivalence translation (which given distinct traits, you wouldn't know because they are inherently not identifiable). In multi-group setups this is possible because we can set one group as identified and freely estimate the other groups, which allows for interpretations relative to this select group, but the same cannot be done across traits because they would not be mathematically identifiable.

>
> Using your new dif function between samples is exciting, i remember reading your effect size paper a while ago. It will be nice to put theory into practice.
>
> To run the three dif models using 2pl with roughly 50 items, what would the minimum sample sizes be to reduce standard error enough for estimates to be meaningful? If we cannot reach that sample size, we might have to simply calculate % correct for each task and group and calculate cohens d. This might give us simikar information without the sample size requirements.

I don't have a hard-limit on sample sizes worked out, but they are asymptotically efficient statistics. So, worst case you'll likely have under-powered tests if the SE is too high, and that may be all you can say about the analysis until you get more data. Re: computing cohen's d, that's not the same thing as bias. That approach would include both the latent trait difference AND bias at the same time, so a large cohen's d could be because a) the groups have population differences, b) the item has compensatory DIF, or c) both. If an item has a small cohens d then similar problems arise. Hence, bias is not something about the observed data; you need to account for unobserved distribution differences in the traits first before inspecting whether any bias response is suspect.

Phil

Say I have an item bank with 9 items, 5-point scale. And there is no testlet (bundle) in the item bank. One-dimension.

mod <- multipleGroup(dat, model, group=group, SE=TRUE,

You have to keep in mind sampling error affects these plots. So although you are seeing potentially large functional differences the parameter estimates are too variable, and can dramatically change in new samples. Hence, raw observations are not always reliable, which is why we have statistical tests.

> 2. After multipleGroup(), if I want to see if the identified 3 DIF items are significant at the test level (i.e. clinical significance), should I just proceed with DRF()? Basically what I used as the codes are:

If they fix the traits to 0 then these effectively drop out of the model. Anything times 0 is 0, so the equation

P(y = k) = logit(a1 * theta1 + a2 * theta2 + .... + ak * thetak + d)

would simplify to

P(y = k) = logit(a1 * theta1 + d)

if all theta2 to thetak = 0. There's no difference in interpretation.

sv$value[sv$name == 'a1'] <- general_slopes
sv$value[sv$name == 'd'] <- intercepts

unidim <- mirt(data, 1, pars = sv)

messages.subject: Linking without common items or persons
messages.subject_clean: Linking without common items or persons
messages.body_plain:
Hi Phil,

I have a question not directly related to the package, but more to (M)IRT in general. Let me describe the situation: I have an operational CAT with an itembank of about 200 items measuring numerical ability. I also have a fixed, regular numerical ability test consisting of 25 items; the items are completely different from the ones in the item bank (so no common items). Now, we want to create a parallel test for the fixed test, by using items from the itembank.

However, the problem is that the parameters of the itembank are calibrated on a different sample than the parameters of the fixed test. Consequently, the parameters of the itembank and fixed test are on different metrics and need to be linked. But since we don't have common items (or persons), there is no way to do this within the IRT framework (right?).

Would you have any suggestions on how to link the parameters given the described situation? And would the large difference in the number of items (200 vs. 25) be a problem in the linking process (whatever method is chosen)?

Best,

Dirk

and would like to ask a few questions about the MIRT results and how to compare the results to those of STATA and IRTPRO.

Q1.  Why are there four sets for the estimates of a and c while there are only three in the other two programs?  I think one category would serve as the reference.  If so, which category does MIRT use as the reference?

Yue Hui.
